verdict.reasoning: Patient says, "I'm kind of struggling to breathe at the moment. I got stung by a wasp" linking breathing difficulty with the insect sting.

Sting: "I got stung by a wasp" / "it was one of the two" (bee or wasp). Timing: "it was, just a few minutes ago." Location: "Yeah, it was on my arm." Rash and puncture: patient describes "slightly red" with "a bit of a... hole there" and doctor calls it a "puncture mark." Mild soreness is implied by "it's just a bit sore" when describing lip but not explicitly arm; overall description of local erythematous rash and puncture is supported, soreness at sting site is a mild inference.

Patient: "there's a bit of swelling in my lips. My tongue feels a bit weird" and later "I don't feel like it's particularly acute" regarding breathing, indicating earlier shortness of breath that is not severe now.
Patient: "I'm feeling like slightly anxious" and "I'm just kind of a bit anxious that it might get a bit worse. I just wanted to speak to someone."

Eczema: Patient: "I've had eczema before." Anxiety: Doctor asks about anxiety/panic attacks; patient replies, "yeah, sometimes, occasionally." Medication: When asked, "Have you ever been on medication for that?" patient answers, "Um, no."

Antihistamines: Patient confirms none taken yet — "Not at the moment, no. Nothing, nothing yet." However, current use of other medications is never asked or documented, so stating "not currently taking any medications" adds information not in the transcript.

Doctor asks about family history of illnesses or acute reactions; patient: "not that I think is particularly relevant, no. I don't have any." That supports no known family history of anaphylaxis/acute reactions.
Occupation: Patient: "I am a computer scientist." Living situation: Doctor: "you living alone?" Patient: "Yes." Pet: Patient: "I have a cat, at home."
Doctor: "Your breathing seems all right to me right now" and patient is conversing in full sentences, indicating unlaboured breathing with normal speech.

Doctor: "your lips don't seem swollen to me right now" and after oropharyngeal inspection has no comment of swelling and reassures, "I don't feel that you're having a life-threatening allergic reaction" and later notes absence of airway compromise, supporting no observed swelling of lips, tongue, or oropharynx.

Doctor views arm: "That looks OK to me right now" and queries swelling; patient: "Not particularly... just a bit kind of blotchy, and a bit of a rash. It doesn't feel like particularly swollen." Earlier: "slightly red" and "a bit of a... hole there" (puncture mark). No mention of heat, supporting mild erythema/blotchiness, puncture, and no obvious swelling or heat.

Doctor: "it seems to me like this is a localised allergic reaction" and "I don't feel that you're having a life-threatening allergic reaction" and emphasizes no current compromise of breathing, supporting no systemic reaction/anaphylaxis.

Patient repeatedly expresses worry: "I'm feeling like slightly anxious" and "I'm just kind of a bit anxious that it might get a bit worse"; doctor focuses on ruling out anaphylaxis, consistent with health anxiety about possible anaphylaxis.

Doctor: "What I'd like you to do now, is I'd like you to try and take some antihistamines... you can get Piriton or Chlorphenamine, and you can take one tablet, four milligrams, up to about six times a day. Or you can just take a one-a-day one." This matches chlorphenamine 4 mg PO every 4–6 hours PRN or once-daily alternative.

Doctor gives red-flag advice but directs to A&E, not 999: "if it's progressing rapidly, it's better to go straight to A and E" and "either make an appointment with us, or go straight to A and E." There is no mention of calling 999, so "requires immediate 999/ED contact" introduces 999, which is not in the transcript.

Doctor: "if the redness in your arm spreads, and it feels hot, or you have signs of any localised infection. We may need to think about other treatments, like an antibiotic." This aligns with monitoring the site and seeking review if spreading erythema, heat, or pain suggesting possible infection.

Doctor: "I'm gonna leave a link to some information about anaphylactic reactions, just for you to read about it. I don't want you to panic, but just for you to be aware what symptoms are." and "If you're feeling worried, just have a lower threshold for having a chat with us" plus discussion of possible future testing if recurrent, supporting information link, reassurance, and encouragement to re-contact if symptoms change or recur.
